slides.title: Phenomenology
points: Understand lived experience and the meaning of a phenomenon
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of phenomenology
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Explore how people experience a phenomenon
Describe or interpret its meaning
Focus on experience rather than frequency

slides.title: Philosophical foundations
points: Introduce intentionality and the lifeworld
Contrast Husserlian description with Heideggerian interpretation
Explain why philosophical commitments shape methods

slides.title: Descriptive and interpretive traditions
points: Descriptive work seeks an account of essential experiential features
Interpretive work examines situated meaning
Name and justify the tradition chosen

slides.title: When to use phenomenology
points: Choose an experience shared by participants
Use when meanings remain poorly understood
Avoid questions primarily seeking a process theory

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Ask what an experience is like or how it is understood
Specify the phenomenon and population
Avoid imposing predetermined categories

slides.title: Illustrative study question
points: Hypothetical example: living with newly diagnosed glaucoma
Ask how diagnosis changes everyday perception and identity
Keep the focus on lived experience

slides.title: Researcher position and reflexivity
points: State relevant clinical or personal experience
Examine assumptions about the phenomenon
Record how researcher-participant relationships shape interpretation

slides.title: Bracketing and prior understanding
points: Descriptive traditions examine and suspend assumptions where possible
Interpretive traditions critically engage prior understanding
Explain that complete neutrality is not attainable

slides.title: Participant selection
points: Recruit people with direct experience of the phenomenon
Use purposive criteria aligned with the question
Consider experiential variation without losing a shared focus

slides.title: Sample adequacy
points: Seek rich experiential accounts
Justify sample size by scope, depth and analytic tradition
Avoid a universal numerical rule or unexamined saturation claim

slides.title: Interview design
points: Invite concrete accounts of particular situations
Probe bodily, temporal and relational experience
Use open prompts without leading explanations

slides.title: Additional experiential materials
points: Consider diaries, drawings and written reflections
Explain what each material contributes
Obtain consent for personal artifacts

slides.title: Data preparation
points: Transcribe faithfully and de-identify accounts
Preserve contextual details needed for meaning
Re-read each account as a whole

slides.title: Selecting an analytic approach
points: Describe options such as Giorgi, Colaizzi or van Manen
Align procedures with philosophical commitments
Avoid treating different traditions as interchangeable recipes

slides.title: Meaning units and experiential patterns
points: Identify passages relevant to the phenomenon
Explore how meanings relate across accounts
Keep interpretation anchored in concrete experiences

slides.title: Developing an experiential account
points: Describe what was experienced and how it was experienced
Examine shared features and meaningful variation
Use essential structure only where the tradition supports it

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical excerpt: uncertainty before the next eye examination
Identify altered time and bodily vigilance as possible meanings
Show the interpretive steps without presenting invented results as evidence

slides.title: Quality and credibility
points: Demonstrate methodological coherence and depth
Use rich excerpts and a transparent analytic account
Consider participant feedback where appropriate to the tradition

slides.title: Ethics and sensitive experiences
points: Anticipate distress when discussing illness or loss
Allow pauses and withdrawal
Protect identity in detailed experiential narratives

slides.title: Reporting the study
points: Explain tradition, researcher position and analytic choices
Present experiential descriptions supported by excerpts
Relate findings to the phenomenon without claiming prevalence

slides.title: Strengths, limitations and common errors
points: Provides depth about meaning and experience
Interpretation depends on context and researcher engagement
Avoid relabeling a generic thematic interview study as phenomenology

slides.title: Key takeaways and discussion
points: Align philosophy, question and analytic method
Prioritize concrete lived accounts and reflexivity
Discuss whether an experience question fits this design

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Creswell & Poth. Qualitative Inquiry and Research Design, 5th ed. SAGE. https://us2.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design/book266033
slides.visual: Readable reference list with source links

slides.title: Grounded theory
points: Develop an explanatory theory of a social process
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of grounded theory
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and intended product
points: Develop theory grounded in systematically analyzed data
Explain actions, interactions or social processes
Produce linked concepts rather than a list of themes

slides.title: Origins and theoretical roots
points: Introduce Glaser and Strauss and the emergence of grounded theory
Explain the role of symbolic interactionism in many approaches
Note later methodological developments

slides.title: Major grounded theory traditions
points: Compare classic, Straussian and constructivist approaches
Examine differences in researcher role and analytic procedures
Choose one coherent approach for the study

slides.title: When grounded theory fits
points: Use when a process lacks an adequate explanation
Focus on how people act under changing conditions
Assess whether theory generation is the intended outcome

slides.title: Formulating a process question
points: Ask how a process unfolds
Define the initial population and context
Leave room to revise the question as analysis develops

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: adapting to long-term eye-drop treatment
Explore how patients negotiate routines and setbacks
Aim to explain adaptation rather than only describe barriers

slides.title: Researcher position and sensitizing concepts
points: Declare relevant experience and assumptions
Use sensitizing concepts as starting points rather than fixed codes
Examine how interaction shapes the data

slides.title: Initial purposive sampling
points: Begin with participants likely to illuminate the process
Seek useful variation in experience or circumstances
Explain how initial sampling differs from later theoretical sampling

slides.title: Theoretical sampling
points: Select additional people, events or documents to develop categories
Let emerging analytic questions guide recruitment
Document why each next source was chosen

slides.title: Concurrent collection and analysis
points: Analyze early interviews before collecting all data
Adapt questions to emerging concepts
Maintain an iterative relationship between fieldwork and analysis

slides.title: Data collection methods
points: Use intensive interviews, observation or relevant documents
Ask about actions and changes over time
Follow up unclear sequences and decisions

slides.title: Initial coding
points: Code close to the data in manageable segments
Use action-focused labels where consistent with the approach
Compare alternative interpretations of the same incident

slides.title: Focused coding and category development
points: Select analytically useful codes
Group and refine codes into categories
Specify properties and dimensions of categories

slides.title: Axial and relational analysis
points: Straussian approaches examine relationships among categories
Other traditions use different relational procedures
Avoid imposing a universal coding sequence on every approach

slides.title: Constant comparative analysis
points: Compare incidents with incidents, codes and categories
Examine similarities, differences and exceptions
Refine concepts throughout collection and analysis

slides.title: Memo writing
points: Record analytic ideas and unanswered questions
Explain connections and category boundaries
Use memos to guide theoretical sampling and writing

slides.title: Theoretical integration
points: Identify a central process or integrative explanation where appropriate
Link categories into an explanatory account
Check that relationships are supported by data

slides.title: Theoretical sufficiency and saturation
points: Assess whether categories and relationships are adequately developed
Seek unresolved variation or negative cases
Justify stopping with evidence rather than interview count alone

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical path: missing doses, simplifying routines and seeking support
Develop possible categories about negotiating treatment burden
Show how new interviews could challenge the proposed explanation

slides.title: Quality and reflexivity
points: Evaluate coherence, grounding and explanatory usefulness
Maintain an audit trail of comparisons and sampling decisions
State quality criteria consistent with the chosen tradition

slides.title: Ethics in an evolving design
points: Explain adaptive recruitment and interview changes
Obtain amendments when required by the approved protocol
Protect participants in small networks

slides.title: Reporting, limitations and takeaways
points: Report sampling evolution, coding, memos and the final model
Avoid presenting thematic analysis alone as grounded theory
Discuss the scope and transferability of the explanation

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Charmaz. Constructing Grounded Theory. SAGE. https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/constructing-grounded-theory-3-255601
Charmaz. Teaching Theory Construction With Initial Grounded Theory Tools. https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732315613982

slides.title: Ethnography
points: Understand shared meanings and practices within a cultural setting
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of ethnography
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Study everyday practices and shared meanings in context
Examine how a group organizes social life
Connect observed behavior with cultural interpretation

slides.title: Intellectual roots
points: Introduce anthropology and sociological fieldwork
Explain interpretive and critical developments
Recognize the legacy of colonial representation

slides.title: Forms of ethnography
points: Compare conventional, focused, critical and digital ethnography
Distinguish scope and field relations
Explain why short observation alone is not enough to establish ethnography

slides.title: When ethnography fits
points: Use when routines, tacit norms or group practices matter
Choose a setting where observation adds essential evidence
Assess feasibility of meaningful field engagement

slides.title: Framing the research question
points: Ask how people enact and understand practices in a setting
Define a provisional cultural focus
Keep room for unexpected field discoveries

slides.title: Illustrative study setting
points: Hypothetical example: teamwork in an ophthalmology clinic
Explore handover routines, professional hierarchy and patient flow
Examine formal rules alongside everyday practice

slides.title: Selecting the field and boundaries
points: Define sites, actors and relevant activities
Consider multiple connected locations when needed
State temporal and organizational boundaries

slides.title: Access and gatekeepers
points: Negotiate entry with responsible organizations
Seek consent beyond gatekeeper permission
Explain how access conditions may shape what is observed

slides.title: Researcher roles in the field
points: Compare participant and non-participant observation
Explain insider and outsider positions
Consider how role changes affect relationships and data

slides.title: Sampling people, events and times
points: Select key informants and varied perspectives
Observe different shifts, routines and exceptional events
Revise sampling as cultural patterns emerge

slides.title: Immersion and field engagement
points: Spend enough time to understand recurring practices
Develop familiarity without assuming complete membership
Justify duration in relation to scope and access

slides.title: Participant observation
points: Observe actions, interactions and material arrangements
Record what happens as well as what people say should happen
Separate descriptive records from interpretive impressions

slides.title: Fieldnotes
points: Capture scenes, dialogue, setting and researcher responses
Expand brief notes promptly
Keep analytic and reflexive notes identifiable

slides.title: Ethnographic interviewing
points: Use informal conversations and more focused interviews
Ask participants to explain locally meaningful terms
Compare accounts with observed practices

slides.title: Artifacts and digital materials
points: Analyze forms, spaces, tools and online interactions
Ask how material objects organize activity
Respect permissions for images and digital access

slides.title: Emic and etic perspectives
points: Distinguish participants' understandings from analytic interpretation
Explain local categories before applying external concepts
Move critically between perspectives

slides.title: Ethnographic analysis
points: Organize field records and identify recurring practices
Develop cultural themes and relationships
Revisit the field to investigate puzzles and exceptions

slides.title: Thick description
points: Describe action alongside context and local meaning
Explain why a practice matters to participants
Avoid confusing detail alone with cultural interpretation

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical observation: junior staff rarely challenge a senior's instructions
Compare interviews, fieldnotes and organizational rules
Explore hierarchy while seeking situations that contradict the pattern

slides.title: Reflexivity, ethics and representation
points: Examine positionality and changing field relationships
Manage ongoing consent and incidental bystanders
Avoid stereotypes and protect recognizable groups

slides.title: Quality, strengths and limitations
points: Use sustained engagement, contextual evidence and negative cases
Explain access limits and researcher influence
Avoid treating one group as representative of an entire population

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Integrate scenes, participant language and cultural interpretation
Describe field access and analytic decisions
Discuss how observed practices connect with local meanings

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Creswell & Poth. Qualitative Inquiry and Research Design, 5th ed. SAGE. https://us2.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design/book266033
slides.visual: Readable reference list with source links

slides.title: Case study
points: Examine a bounded case in depth within its real-world context
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of case study
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Investigate a bounded case within its context
Integrate multiple sources of evidence
Clarify that case studies may be qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods

slides.title: Methodological orientations
points: Introduce Yin, Stake and Merriam as influential approaches
Contrast explanatory and interpretive emphases
Align the case-study tradition with the research aim

slides.title: What counts as a case
points: A case may be a person, program, organization, event or process
Specify its unit of analysis
Distinguish the case from participants interviewed within it

slides.title: Bounding the case
points: Define time, place, activity and organizational limits
State what is included and excluded
Keep boundaries aligned with the question

slides.title: When case study fits
points: Use for context-dependent how or why questions
Examine a contemporary or otherwise bounded phenomenon in depth
Choose another design if case boundaries have no analytic role

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Link the question to the bounded case
Specify what must be understood or explained
Introduce propositions only where the tradition requires them

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: implementing teleophthalmology at one hospital
Bound the implementation to a defined period and service
Examine organizational influences on adoption

slides.title: Intrinsic, instrumental and collective cases
points: Intrinsic work prioritizes the particular case
Instrumental work uses a case to understand a broader issue
Collective work examines several cases around an issue

slides.title: Single and multiple-case designs
points: Justify depth in one case or comparison across cases
Select multiple cases for meaningful conceptual comparison
Avoid treating convenience alone as a full design rationale

slides.title: Holistic and embedded units
points: Holistic designs study the case as a whole
Embedded designs analyze subunits within the case
Keep subunit findings connected to the overall case

slides.title: Case selection
points: Consider critical, typical, unusual or contrasting cases
Explain the logic of selection
Distinguish conceptual selection from statistical sampling

slides.title: Participant and document sampling
points: Recruit people with different relationships to the case
Select relevant records and observation opportunities
Track missing perspectives or inaccessible evidence

slides.title: Case-study protocol
points: Specify questions, access, sources and collection procedures
Use consistent procedures where comparisons require them
Adapt responsibly to field conditions

slides.title: Multiple sources of evidence
points: Combine interviews, observation, records and artifacts as appropriate
Explain what each source can establish
Do not equate source quantity with automatic credibility

slides.title: Case database and chain of evidence
points: Organize records and preserve source identifiers
Trace claims to evidence and analytic decisions
Separate raw materials from interpretive summaries

slides.title: Within-case analysis
points: Build a detailed account of the case
Examine chronology, patterns and contextual relationships
Analyze discrepant evidence rather than forcing consensus

slides.title: Explanation building and rival accounts
points: Compare possible explanations for observed outcomes
Test patterns against supporting and contradicting evidence
State the limits of causal inference

slides.title: Cross-case synthesis
points: Develop each case account before comparison
Compare themes or explanatory patterns across cases
Preserve meaningful contextual differences

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical evidence links uptake to workflow integration and staff support
Compare policy documents, interviews and observations
Examine alternative explanations such as equipment access

slides.title: Quality and reflexivity
points: Use criteria consistent with the selected tradition
Make boundaries, evidence and interpretations transparent
Explain researcher access and assumptions

slides.title: Ethics, strengths and limitations
points: Protect a potentially identifiable organization and staff
Balance contextual depth with disclosure risk
Distinguish analytic transferability from population estimates

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Describe the case, boundaries, methods and context
Integrate evidence into a coherent account
Discuss what the case illuminates beyond its immediate setting

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Yin. Case Study Research and Applications, 6th ed. SAGE. https://study.sagepub.com/yin6e
Creswell & Poth. Qualitative Inquiry and Research Design. https://us2.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design/book266033
slides.visual: Readable reference list with source links

slides.title: Narrative inquiry
points: Explore how people construct and communicate experience through stories
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of narrative inquiry
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Investigate experience as narrated and interpreted
Explore identity, sequence and meaning in stories
Preserve the relationship between events and their telling

slides.title: Conceptual foundations
points: Introduce narrative construction and situated meaning
Explain temporal, social and spatial dimensions of experience
Recognize that stories are shaped for audiences

slides.title: Forms of narrative research
points: Compare life histories, illness narratives and focused personal accounts
Consider oral, written and visual stories
Choose the form that answers the research question

slides.title: When narrative inquiry fits
points: Use for identity development, transitions or turning points
Seek an account of experience across time
Avoid fragmenting stories when their sequence is central

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Ask how participants narrate a transition or construct identity
Specify whose stories and which period matter
Consider the context and audience of the telling

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: a physician's transition into a new healthcare system
Explore belonging, uncertainty and professional identity over time
Treat the telling as part of the data

slides.title: Selecting participants and stories
points: Use purposive selection for rich relevant accounts
Decide whether to study one or several narrators
Justify depth and variation without a universal sample rule

slides.title: Building research relationships
points: Establish trust while acknowledging researcher influence
Negotiate expectations around interpretation and representation
Recognize stories as produced within a relationship

slides.title: Narrative interview design
points: Begin with invitations to tell a story
Ask follow-ups about episodes and turning points
Limit interruption during an unfolding account

slides.title: Temporal prompts and life maps
points: Use timelines to locate significant periods and events
Ask how interpretations changed over time
Keep chronology distinct from the order in which a story is told

slides.title: Additional narrative materials
points: Consider diaries, letters, photographs and digital stories
Ask participants to explain their significance
Verify permission and authorship of materials

slides.title: Transcription and representation
points: Preserve pauses, emphasis or sequencing when analytically relevant
State conventions used
Recognize transcription as an interpretive decision

slides.title: Reconstructing the narrative context
points: Identify setting, actors, audience and circumstances
Distinguish narrated events from present-day interpretation
Preserve uncertainty and conflicting recollections

slides.title: Thematic narrative analysis
points: Examine what a story is about
Analyze content within whole-case narratives
Compare accounts without losing each story's context

slides.title: Structural narrative analysis
points: Examine how a story is organized and told
Identify plot, sequence and evaluative elements
Explain how form contributes to meaning

slides.title: Dialogic and performance analysis
points: Examine who tells the story, to whom and for what purpose
Analyze positioning and interaction during the telling
Consider social narratives and available identities

slides.title: Visual narrative analysis
points: Explore how images and accompanying accounts construct a story
Consider composition, sequence and participant interpretation
Avoid interpreting images without their context

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical account moves from confidence to disorientation to renewed belonging
Compare event chronology with narrative structure
Ask what identity the narrator constructs for the audience

slides.title: Reflexivity and researcher voice
points: Examine how questions shape the story told
Make interpretive choices visible
Distinguish participant words from researcher reconstruction

slides.title: Ethics and relational responsibilities
points: Negotiate identifiable life details and third-party portrayals
Discuss consent for quotations and images
Revisit consent as representation develops

slides.title: Quality, strengths and limitations
points: Support interpretation with coherent narrative evidence
Consider participant dialogue where appropriate
Discuss memory, audience effects and limits of retrospective accounts

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Present stories with sufficient temporal and social context
Explain the selected analytic approach
Discuss how storytelling constructs meaning and identity

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Riessman. Narrative Methods for the Human Sciences. SAGE. https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/narrative-methods-for-the-human-sciences-1-226139
Creswell & Poth. Qualitative Inquiry and Research Design. https://us2.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design/book266033
slides.visual: Readable reference list with source links

slides.title: Qualitative descriptive study
points: Provide a clear, practice-relevant description in everyday terms
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of qualitative descriptive study
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Provide a comprehensive account of an event or experience
Stay close to participants' everyday terms
Use interpretation while keeping the level of abstraction relatively low

slides.title: Methodological orientation
points: Explain a naturalistic orientation and attention to context
Use flexible methods suited to the question
Avoid claiming that description is entirely interpretation-free

slides.title: Distinctive features
points: Prioritize accessible descriptions and practical questions
Seek an organized account of participants' perspectives
Do not require theory generation or a phenomenological essence

slides.title: When qualitative description fits
points: Use for needs, barriers, preferences and service experiences
Choose when a direct practical account is the intended outcome
Assess whether more interpretive designs are needed

slides.title: Distinguishing adjacent approaches
points: Compare descriptive aims with phenomenology and grounded theory
Contrast everyday categories with higher conceptual abstraction
State why a descriptive approach meets the objective

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Use focused what or how questions
Identify the population and practical issue
Avoid building an explanatory theory claim into a descriptive aim

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: patients' barriers to glaucoma follow-up
Describe logistical, informational and interpersonal difficulties
Explore helpful service changes from participants' perspectives

slides.title: Researcher position
points: Describe the researcher's relationship to the setting
Reflect on assumptions about patient needs
Keep a record of decisions that affect description

slides.title: Sampling strategy
points: Use purposive or maximum-variation sampling where appropriate
Seek perspectives relevant to the practical question
Explain inclusion criteria and recruitment channels

slides.title: Sample adequacy
points: Consider breadth of perspectives and depth of accounts
Assess whether the data answer the focused question
Justify stopping without imposing a universal number

slides.title: Semi-structured interviews
points: Use open questions with practical probes
Ask for concrete examples and proposed improvements
Pilot the guide for clarity and accessibility

slides.title: Focus groups
points: Explore shared and differing perspectives through interaction
Consider how hierarchy or stigma affects speaking
Explain when individual interviews are preferable

slides.title: Observation and documents
points: Use observations or materials when they clarify the service context
Link sources to the question
Distinguish observed events from reported experiences

slides.title: Preparing the data
points: Transcribe, organize and de-identify records
Preserve relevant context and participant language
Document translation and transcription decisions

slides.title: Qualitative content analysis
points: Select a content-analysis approach suited to the aim
Develop categories systematically from relevant data
Explain whether categories are inductive, deductive or combined

slides.title: Coding and category development
points: Assign clear labels to meaningful segments
Group related codes into descriptive categories
Define category boundaries and revise them with new evidence

slides.title: Using summaries and matrices
points: Compare categories across participants and contexts
Preserve variation and contradictory accounts
Use matrices to organize rather than replace interpretation

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical comments describe transport costs and unclear appointment instructions
Build distinct categories with supporting excerpts
Avoid interpreting convenience-selected counts as population prevalence

slides.title: Reflexivity and analytic transparency
points: Record how categories were developed
Discuss interpretive disagreements constructively
Explain how prior assumptions influenced analysis

slides.title: Credibility and transferability
points: Support categories with adequate evidence
Describe setting and recruitment clearly
Seek feedback or additional evidence where useful

slides.title: Ethics, strengths and limitations
points: Protect participants discussing dissatisfaction with services
Produce accessible findings for practical use
Recognize limited explanatory depth relative to theory-focused aims

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Present clear categories, variation and relevant excerpts
Separate findings from proposed service implications
Explain why qualitative description fits the intended product

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Sandelowski M. Whatever happened to qualitative description? Research in Nursing & Health. 2000;23(4):334-340. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10940958/
slides.visual: Readable reference list with source links

slides.title: Participatory action research
points: Co-produce knowledge and action with people affected by the issue
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of participatory action research
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Combine collective inquiry with action for change
Involve affected people as research partners
Explain that participatory action research can use qualitative and quantitative methods

slides.title: Foundations and values
points: Introduce democratic participation and critical reflection
Examine power, inequality and situated knowledge
Treat practical and experiential expertise as important knowledge

slides.title: PAR and action research
points: PAR places explicit emphasis on shared ownership and participation
Action research is a broader family of iterative inquiry
Recognize overlap rather than a rigid boundary

slides.title: When PAR fits
points: Use when affected groups should shape research and change
Assess readiness for a sustained partnership
Avoid adopting a participatory label for consultation alone

slides.title: Identifying partners and stakeholders
points: Map who experiences the problem and who holds resources
Include marginalized voices and relevant decision-makers
Clarify differences between stakeholders and co-researchers

slides.title: Building the partnership
points: Discuss expectations, trust and prior experiences
Agree on compensation, roles and ways of working
Invest time before finalizing the research agenda

slides.title: Shared governance
points: Co-develop decision-making and conflict-resolution procedures
Agree who controls budgets, data and dissemination
Make accountability visible throughout the project

slides.title: Co-defining the research question
points: Ask partners which problems matter most
Negotiate a feasible question and action goal
Record how priorities were chosen

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: community barriers to glaucoma screening
Residents and staff jointly identify access priorities
Frame both an inquiry question and a change objective

slides.title: Researcher positionality and power
points: Examine institutional privilege and unequal influence
Make assumptions and constraints open for discussion
Create ways to challenge researcher decisions

slides.title: Recruitment and inclusive participation
points: Use accessible recruitment and meeting formats
Address language, transport, disability and time barriers
Monitor whose perspectives remain absent

slides.title: Co-designing data collection
points: Choose interviews, observation, mapping or other methods together
Train co-researchers and pilot tools collaboratively
Match methods to both inquiry and action goals

slides.title: Participatory methods
points: Consider photovoice, community mapping and collective story gathering
Discuss strengths and disclosure risks
Explain how participants help interpret the material

slides.title: The inquiry and action cycle
points: Identify the issue, plan action, act, observe and reflect
Treat cycles as flexible rather than mechanical
Revise questions and activities through collective learning

slides.title: Collaborative analysis
points: Make data accessible to co-researchers in appropriate forms
Discuss interpretations and disagreements together
Document whose perspectives shape conclusions

slides.title: From findings to action
points: Translate jointly interpreted evidence into priorities
Assign responsibilities and feasible resources
Distinguish recommended actions from actions actually implemented

slides.title: Implementing change
points: Pilot agreed activities and document adaptations
Track participation and unintended consequences
Preserve shared decision-making during implementation

slides.title: Evaluating process and outcomes
points: Assess partnership quality as well as practical changes
Agree indicators with partners
Use qualitative and quantitative evidence where helpful

slides.title: Worked project example
points: Hypothetical cycle identifies inaccessible appointment times
Partners pilot an agreed scheduling change and collect feedback
Reflect jointly before deciding the next cycle

slides.title: Ethics and ownership
points: Negotiate consent, confidentiality and data stewardship
Address collective and individual interests
Agree authorship, recognition and dissemination rights

slides.title: Quality, strengths and limitations
points: Evaluate participation, relevance and transparent learning
Recognize resource demands and power tensions
Avoid equating immediate success with rigorous inquiry

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Report partner roles, decisions, cycles and outcomes
Share findings in forms useful to the community
Discuss whether participation changed both knowledge and action

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Baum F, MacDougall C, Smith D. Participatory action research. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health. 2006;60:854-857. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16973531/
Kemmis, McTaggart & Nixon. The Action Research Planner. Springer. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-4560-67-2

slides.title: Action research
points: Improve a local practice through systematic cycles of inquiry and reflection
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of action research
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Investigate practice while attempting to improve it
Connect action with systematic observation and reflection
Explain that action research may use qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods

slides.title: Roots and orientations
points: Introduce iterative inquiry associated with Lewin
Compare practical, collaborative and critical orientations
Explain how aims shape participation and evidence

slides.title: Distinguishing adjacent activities
points: Compare action research with routine quality improvement and evaluation
Explain the role of systematic inquiry and learning
Recognize overlap and context-dependent boundaries

slides.title: Action research and PAR
points: Both involve inquiry linked to change
PAR explicitly foregrounds shared ownership by affected people
State the actual level of participation instead of relying on a label

slides.title: When action research fits
points: Use for a local practice problem that can be acted on
Ensure access to implementation and observation
Assess whether iterative learning is feasible

slides.title: Identifying the practice problem
points: Gather initial evidence of the problem
Include practitioners' and users' perspectives
Separate assumptions from documented concerns

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Link an improvement goal to an inquiry question
Ask what happens when a defined change is introduced
Define the setting and intended learning

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: improving clarity of glaucoma education
Ask how a revised consultation guide changes communication
Examine patient and staff experiences of the change

slides.title: Setting, team and roles
points: Define the practice context and project team
Clarify practitioner and researcher responsibilities
Record who decides what changes

slides.title: Baseline inquiry
points: Observe existing practice before intervention
Collect interviews, documents or available measures
Use baseline evidence to refine the first action

slides.title: Planning the first cycle
points: Specify the action, rationale and resources
Agree what evidence will be collected
Set criteria for revising or stopping the activity

slides.title: Taking action
points: Implement the agreed practice change
Document fidelity and adaptations
Record practical constraints as data for reflection

slides.title: Observing the effects
points: Collect evidence of experiences, behavior and consequences
Capture unintended effects and contextual changes
Avoid relying only on practitioner impressions

slides.title: Reflecting and revising
points: Compare intended and observed effects
Discuss explanations and alternative actions
Document how reflection changes the next plan

slides.title: Designing subsequent cycles
points: Revise the action based on prior learning
Keep the inquiry question coherent as practice evolves
Explain why cycles differ rather than presenting a fixed recipe

slides.title: Qualitative data collection
points: Use interviews, group discussions, journals and observation
Ask about usability and contextual barriers
Align collection timing with each cycle

slides.title: Using complementary measures
points: Add service indicators or surveys where relevant
State definitions and limitations of measures
Treat counts as supporting evidence rather than automatic causal proof

slides.title: Analysis across cycles
points: Analyze each cycle and compare patterns over time
Link evidence to specific adaptations
Examine alternative explanations for observed change

slides.title: Practitioner reflexivity
points: Consider how investment in success shapes interpretation
Keep reflective records of decisions and tensions
Seek critical perspectives beyond the project team

slides.title: Worked project example
points: Hypothetical first cycle reveals an education guide is too technical
A revised version is tested in a second cycle
Compare feedback without inventing evidence of effectiveness

slides.title: Ethics, quality and limitations
points: Manage power relationships with patients, staff or students
Explain permissions for service changes and research data
Recognize local scope and limits on causal attribution

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Describe problem, actions, evidence, reflection and revisions
Distinguish implementation outcomes from research learning
Discuss what can transfer to another practice setting

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Kemmis, McTaggart & Nixon. The Action Research Planner: Doing Critical Participatory Action Research. Springer. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-4560-67-2

slides.title: Interpretive description
points: Develop contextual interpretations that inform professional practice
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of interpretive description
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and intended product
points: Generate an interpretive account useful for applied practice
Examine patterns alongside individual variation
Move beyond description toward practice-relevant understanding

slides.title: Origins and disciplinary purpose
points: Introduce Thorne and colleagues' nursing-oriented development
Explain the need for applied knowledge distinct from disciplinary theory goals
Recognize use in other professional contexts

slides.title: Philosophical orientation
points: Attend to constructed and contextual experience
Acknowledge multiple realities and researcher interpretation
Explain how disciplinary assumptions influence inquiry

slides.title: Distinctive features
points: Use professional knowledge critically as a starting point
Seek patterns that can inform practice
Preserve exceptions and complexity

slides.title: When interpretive description fits
points: Choose an applied question requiring contextual understanding
Seek meaningful patterns rather than a formal social-process theory
Assess whether findings can support professional judgment

slides.title: Comparing neighboring designs
points: Qualitative description stays relatively close to everyday accounts
Phenomenology centers lived meaning and grounded theory builds theory
Interpretive description pursues applied interpretation

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Ask how experiences or practices vary and why that matters professionally
Identify the clinical or applied problem
Avoid assuming the answer from professional expertise

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: how patients integrate glaucoma monitoring into daily life
Explore different circumstances and needs
Seek insights for individualized follow-up support

slides.title: Reviewing existing knowledge
points: Identify relevant clinical evidence and conceptual assumptions
Use literature to clarify the practical gap
Keep prior knowledge open to challenge by the data

slides.title: Researcher position and disciplinary lens
points: State professional experience and relationships
Examine how expertise guides attention and interpretation
Reflect on assumptions about what counts as useful knowledge

slides.title: Purposive sampling
points: Recruit cases likely to reveal patterns and meaningful variation
Consider experience, circumstances and practice context
Revise selection to investigate emerging interpretations

slides.title: Sample adequacy
points: Judge whether evidence supports the applied interpretation
Seek exceptions and unresolved differences
Justify scope and depth rather than a universal sample count

slides.title: Interviews and focused discussions
points: Invite concrete experiences and practical examples
Probe variation in needs and responses
Avoid making interviews into clinical counseling sessions

slides.title: Observation and supporting sources
points: Observe relevant interactions or routines when feasible
Use documents to understand the practice context
Explain how different sources inform the interpretation

slides.title: Concurrent analytic work
points: Begin analysis while collection continues
Adjust questions to investigate emerging differences
Record changes in the analytic focus

slides.title: Coding without losing context
points: Use codes to organize material rather than define the final findings
Compare accounts within and across cases
Keep personal circumstances attached to interpretations

slides.title: Developing interpretive patterns
points: Ask what patterns mean for the applied problem
Examine relationships among experience, context and responses
Avoid reducing all differences to a single theme

slides.title: Testing interpretations
points: Seek alternative explanations and discrepant cases
Revisit evidence and collect clarifying data when possible
Separate a plausible interpretation from a proven causal mechanism

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical accounts suggest support needs differ by routine flexibility and uncertainty
Compare contrasting cases before proposing a pattern
Show how the interpretation could guide further inquiry

slides.title: Translating findings into practice
points: Explain implications for assessment or communication
Preserve uncertainty and individual variation
Distinguish an interpretive implication from a tested intervention

slides.title: Quality, ethics and limitations
points: Demonstrate coherence, analytic logic and contextual relevance
Protect participants within professional relationships
Recognize researcher influence and limits of untested recommendations

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Describe disciplinary grounding, sampling and analytic decisions
Present interpretations with supporting evidence and exceptions
Discuss how findings inform rather than replace professional judgment

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Thorne S, Kirkham SR, MacDonald-Emes J. Interpretive description: a noncategorical qualitative alternative for developing nursing knowledge. Research in Nursing & Health. 1997;20(2):169-177. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9100747/

slides.title: Discourse analysis
points: Examine how language constructs meaning, identity and social relations
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of discourse analysis
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Analyze language as social action and meaning-making
Examine identities, categories and relationships produced in discourse
Explain that discourse analysis is a family of approaches

slides.title: Conceptual foundations
points: Introduce socially situated meaning and discourse
Explain relationships between language, institutions and power
State the theoretical position guiding analysis

slides.title: Major analytic traditions
points: Compare critical discourse analysis, discursive psychology and Foucauldian approaches
Note distinct assumptions, questions and analytic tools
Avoid combining traditions without justification

slides.title: When discourse analysis fits
points: Use when wording, interaction or representation is central
Examine how a category or claim becomes persuasive
Choose a content-focused design if only topic summaries are needed

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Ask how language constructs an identity, problem or responsibility
Specify the discourse and setting
Identify what linguistic or social process needs examination

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: representations of patient adherence in clinic materials
Ask how responsibility is assigned to patients and services
Examine implications for professional-patient relations

slides.title: Selecting the corpus
points: Define documents, conversations or media to be analyzed
State time period, inclusion criteria and source context
Justify boundaries and exclusions

slides.title: Sampling and corpus adequacy
points: Select material relevant to the discursive question
Seek variation, contrasts or important institutional texts
Assess analytic depth rather than representativeness alone

slides.title: Production and audience context
points: Identify who produced each text and for whom
Examine institutional purpose and circulation
Avoid treating words as detached from their setting

slides.title: Data collection and permissions
points: Collect authentic texts or recorded interactions where suitable
Verify access, copyright and consent
Retain source provenance and versions

slides.title: Transcription detail
points: Match transcription detail to the analytic approach
Preserve pauses or turn-taking when relevant
State how translation may change discursive features

slides.title: Initial reading and analytic notes
points: Read repeatedly for recurring constructions and puzzles
Note contrasts and shifts across contexts
Keep early interpretations provisional

slides.title: Categories, naming and lexical choices
points: Examine labels, pronouns and evaluative terms
Ask which identities and distinctions are created
Link observations to the question and context

slides.title: Agency, grammar and responsibility
points: Examine who is represented as acting or being acted on
Consider active, passive and nominalized constructions
Avoid inferring social effects from grammar alone

slides.title: Metaphor and framing
points: Identify recurring metaphors and problem definitions
Ask what perspectives they enable or obscure
Examine competing framings in the corpus

slides.title: Interpretive repertoires and positioning
points: For relevant traditions, examine recurring ways of talking
Analyze how speakers position themselves and others
Show how these constructions function in particular exchanges

slides.title: Power and ideology
points: In critical approaches, examine authority and inequality
Relate text to institutional and social practices
Support critical claims with evidence rather than assumptions

slides.title: Intertextuality and wider discourses
points: Examine references to other texts and established narratives
Trace how language travels between settings
Consider how prior discourses authorize present claims

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical phrase describes missed visits as patient failure
Compare wording that also names transport and service barriers
Analyze possible constructions without claiming measured effects

slides.title: Analytic transparency and reflexivity
points: Show excerpts and the reasoning behind interpretations
Examine the researcher's own assumptions and language
Consider alternative readings and counterexamples

slides.title: Ethics, strengths and limitations
points: Protect identities in recordings and searchable quotations
Explain limits on inferring private intentions or causal outcomes
Distinguish discourse findings from prevalence estimates

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: State the analytic tradition, corpus and procedures
Present detailed excerpts with contextual interpretation
Discuss what language accomplishes in the selected setting

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Fairclough. Discourse and Social Change. Wiley/Polity. https://www.wiley-vch.de/en?isbn=9780745612188&option=com_eshop&view=product
Riessman. Narrative Methods for the Human Sciences. SAGE. https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/narrative-methods-for-the-human-sciences-1-226139

slides.title: Historical research
points: Reconstruct and interpret past developments through critically assessed evidence
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of historical research
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Investigate change, continuity and meaning in the past
Build interpretations from critically assessed sources
Explain that historical research can include qualitative and quantitative evidence

slides.title: Historical reasoning
points: Distinguish chronology from historical explanation
Consider contingency, context and multiple perspectives
Avoid assuming present categories applied unchanged in the past

slides.title: Forms and orientations
points: Introduce social, institutional, intellectual and oral history
Compare microhistory with broader historical accounts
Select an orientation aligned with the question

slides.title: When historical research fits
points: Use to explain origins and developments across time
Examine how institutions, practices or concepts changed
Assess whether relevant evidence survives and is accessible

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Specify a past phenomenon, period and setting
Ask how or why a development occurred
Keep the question feasible within available sources

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: development of optic disc photography in a defined region
Investigate changes in technology, clinical use and teaching
Bound the inquiry by period and institutions

slides.title: Periodization and boundaries
points: Justify starting and ending dates
Explain significant turning points without assuming inevitable progress
Reassess boundaries as evidence develops

slides.title: Historiography and existing accounts
points: Review how historians have interpreted the topic
Identify disagreements, omissions and evidence gaps
Position the study within those debates

slides.title: Primary and secondary sources
points: Distinguish contemporaneous evidence from later interpretation
Recognize that the distinction depends on the research question
Use both critically rather than treating primary sources as automatically reliable

slides.title: Archival search strategy
points: Identify archives, collections and finding aids
Record search terms, access limits and selection decisions
Plan for incomplete or dispersed records

slides.title: Document provenance
points: Record creator, date, custody and original purpose
Track whether a record is an original, copy or later transcription
Preserve collection and item identifiers

slides.title: External criticism
points: Assess authenticity, authorship and dating
Examine alterations and the transmission of the source
State uncertainties about provenance

slides.title: Internal criticism
points: Assess meaning, purpose, bias and credibility
Consider the author's position and intended audience
Ask what the source could know or reasonably establish

slides.title: Contextual interpretation
points: Read language and actions within their historical setting
Examine institutions and norms of the period
Avoid judging evidence only through present assumptions

slides.title: Corroboration and conflicting sources
points: Compare independent records and perspectives
Investigate discrepancies rather than averaging them away
Distinguish established facts from contested interpretations

slides.title: Archival silences and selection bias
points: Ask whose experiences were recorded or excluded
Consider survival, access and institutional preservation bias
Avoid treating missing records as proof of non-occurrence

slides.title: Oral history
points: Use interviews to study recollection and lived historical meaning
Distinguish memory from contemporaneous records
Explain consent, recording and future archival use

slides.title: Analysis and synthesis
points: Organize evidence by chronology and analytical themes
Examine relationships, continuity and turning points
Maintain a traceable connection between claims and sources

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical sources disagree on when routine photography began
Compare equipment records, teaching materials and recollections
Present a bounded conclusion with unresolved uncertainty

slides.title: Historical explanation and rival accounts
points: Consider technological, institutional and professional explanations
Distinguish temporal sequence from causal evidence
Avoid a single inevitable-progress narrative

slides.title: Ethics, strengths and limitations
points: Respect archive rules and privacy in sensitive records
Recognize unequal representation and incomplete evidence
Address translation, access and interpretation limits

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: State period, sources, source criticism and interpretive choices
Build a coherent account with precise source references
Make uncertainty and competing explanations visible

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Howell & Prevenier. From Reliable Sources: An Introduction to Historical Methods. Cornell University Press. Publisher overview: https://cornellpress.cornell.edu/cornell-university-press-greatest-hits-from-each-decade/

slides.title: Autoethnography
points: Analyze personal experience to understand wider cultural and social life
Core principles, study planning and applied examples
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple topic-related image

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and defining features of autoethnography
Plan sampling, data collection and analysis appropriate to the approach
Evaluate quality, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Use personal experience as material for cultural inquiry
Connect the self with social relationships and institutions
Explain why research analysis is essential beyond personal storytelling

slides.title: Intellectual foundations
points: Introduce reflexive ethnography and situated knowledge
Recognize challenges to detached accounts of research
Examine how researcher identity affects what can be known

slides.title: Forms of autoethnography
points: Compare evocative, analytic, critical and collaborative forms
Explain differences in representation and analytic emphasis
Select a form aligned with the intended contribution

slides.title: When autoethnography fits
points: Use when the researcher's experience offers insight into a cultural issue
Identify a question extending beyond personal recollection
Assess willingness and ethical capacity for self-disclosure

slides.title: Distinguishing autobiography and narrative inquiry
points: Autobiography recounts a life without necessarily conducting cultural analysis
Narrative inquiry may focus on other people's stories
Autoethnography makes the self-culture connection central

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Ask what personal experience reveals about social norms or institutions
Define the cultural setting and issue
Avoid assuming one person's experience represents everyone

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: an international physician adapting to a new clinical culture
Examine language, belonging and institutional expectations
Connect personal episodes with broader professional norms

slides.title: Researcher positionality
points: Describe identity, relationships and institutional location
Examine privilege and vulnerability
Reflect on whose perspectives the account cannot capture

slides.title: Bounding the experience
points: Specify the period, setting and episodes to be examined
Explain why those experiences matter to the question
Distinguish selection criteria from memorable incidents alone

slides.title: Personal records as data
points: Use journals, messages, photographs or recorded reflections where appropriate
Preserve dates and contextual information
Verify permission before including other people's materials

slides.title: Memory work
points: Write detailed recollections and note uncertainty
Compare memories with available records
Treat memory's selectivity as an analytic issue

slides.title: Collecting contextual evidence
points: Use institutional documents, observation or relevant literature
Examine the norms surrounding personal episodes
Avoid treating contextual material as automatic validation of every memory

slides.title: Journaling and reflexive records
points: Record events, emotions and later interpretations separately
Trace changes in understanding over time
Use journals to expose assumptions as well as experiences

slides.title: Selecting significant episodes
points: Choose episodes that illuminate the cultural question
Include contradictions and uncomfortable experiences
Explain the selection process

slides.title: Analytic coding and thematic work
points: Analyze patterns across episodes where appropriate to the chosen form
Examine identity, power and relationships
Keep analytic claims connected to specific experiences

slides.title: Connecting the personal and cultural
points: Ask how institutional norms shape the experience
Examine how the researcher responds to or reproduces those norms
Avoid assuming every personal difficulty has one structural explanation

slides.title: Evocative representation
points: Use scene, dialogue and emotion to convey experience
Make reconstructed dialogue and composite scenes explicit when used
Keep ethical and analytic responsibilities visible

slides.title: Analytic and critical representation
points: Develop explicit cultural or theoretical interpretation where the form requires it
Examine competing explanations
Show how the account contributes beyond the individual

slides.title: Worked analytic example
points: Hypothetical episode concerns hesitation to speak during a team meeting
Compare personal interpretation with contextual norms and alternative readings
Explore belonging and hierarchy without claiming universal behavior

slides.title: Relational ethics and consent
points: Consider people who appear in the researcher's story
Negotiate consent and disguise identifiable details responsibly
Recognize that pseudonyms may not prevent recognition

slides.title: Quality, self-disclosure and limitations
points: Assess coherence, reflexivity, cultural insight and evidence appropriate to the form
Set boundaries around sensitive disclosure
Discuss selective memory and limits of transferability

slides.title: Reporting and key takeaways
points: Explain data, researcher position, analytic form and representation choices
Integrate lived episodes with cultural understanding
Discuss how the self becomes a site of inquiry

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Ellis C, Adams TE, Bochner AP. Autoethnography: An Overview. Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung / Forum: Qualitative Social Research. 12(1). https://doi.org/10.17169/fqs-12.1.1589
